summary.oneLiner: Avenue Supermarts Limited (DMart) is a national value-retailing supermarket chain built on the Everyday Low Cost / Everyday Low Price (EDLC/EDLP) principle.
summary.business: DMart is a national supermarket chain focused on value-retailing, offering a wide range of products across the Foods, Non-Foods (FMCG) and General Merchandise & Apparel categories. Since its first store in Mumbai in 2002 it has grown to 500 stores with 20.58 million sq. ft. of retail business area across 15 states, 1 union territory and NCR, supported by a network of distribution centres and packing centres. Its store offerings aim to provide one-stop shop convenience for customers' everyday shopping needs in a modern ambience with the feel of a large retail mall.

risks.risk: Erosion of the EDLC/EDLP price advantage
risks.note: If the Company is unable to continue offering daily low prices under its Everyday Low Cost / Everyday Low Price strategy, it risks losing its distinct advantage and a substantial portion of its customers, adversely affecting business, financial condition and results of operations. BRSR adds that competitive intensity can adversely affect the strategy as more players adopt similar business models, and that pricing pressure from existing retailers, E-retailers and prospective entrants may impact the business.

risks.risk: Availability of commercially viable real estate for new stores
risks.note: Growth is store-led, so it depends on securing suitable locations, timely execution of sale deeds / leave and license registrations, and obtaining regulatory approvals for those properties - a direct constraint on the pace of expansion.

risks.risk: Execution of store expansion into newer locations, cities and states
risks.note: Management explicitly flags effective management of store expansion and operations in newer geographies; the cluster-based model has to be transplanted into markets where local knowledge and supply-chain density are not yet built.

risks.risk: Attracting, hiring, training and retaining skilled employees
risks.note: The model is labour-intensive across stores and distribution centres. BRSR notes that while junior-to-mid-level talent is continuously available given industry advantages, there are at times challenges in hiring industry-appropriate senior leadership positions.
Inability to maintain an optimal level of inventory in stores may adversely impact operations - a working-capital and availability risk in a high-throughput, low-margin format.

risks.risk: Reading and adapting to changing consumer preferences
risks.note: Continued understanding and prediction of consumers' changing needs and preferences, and timely customising of offerings and assortment, is flagged as a key business risk.

Any breach of cyber security measures could potentially result in disruption of business operations, which run on IT systems covering cash management, in-store, logistics, financial, HR, project management and maintenance functions.

Climate change may result in lower sales, lesser profits and/or increased investments in the short to medium term, and any potential change in climate-related regulations may lead to higher cost of compliance. BRSR identifies extreme weather events disrupting operations, value-chain impact on supply and sourcing partners raising product cost and hurting availability, and challenges in resource availability including water.
The outbreak of any pandemic could materially and adversely affect business, financial condition and results of operations - a footfall-dependent, physical-store exposure.

one-line thesis: First call under new CEO Anshul Asawa, and he used it to do two things DMart has historically avoided: put a public number on store growth (**~15% of the store base per year**, down from the ~20% actually delivered in FY26) and admit the online business had been scaling losses, not scaling economics — **DMart Ready has retreated from 18 cities to 11**, with AEL posting a **INR307 cr net loss** on 17% sales growth. FY26 itself was a strong top line (**~INR67,000 cr, +16%**) with a flat EBITDA margin (**7.8%**) because a **33% employee-cost step-up** (wage code + deliberate "ahead of the curve" capability build) ate the 16bps gross-margin gain and pushed PAT margin down 25bps. Management effectively conceded that **metro same-store growth is structurally capped at last year's ~8%** — so the growth algorithm from here is square footage, not throughput.

> **Adjustments / one-offs to call out explicitly:**
> 1. **The 13 / 19 / 15 quarterly revenue sequence is a price artefact, not a demand trend.** Management attributed the 13% Dec quarter to **deflation in grocery/staples**, and the 19% March quarter partly to **panic buying in March 2026** — which then *spilled over into* the June quarter. Read the three together, not separately.
> 2. **Employee cost rose 33% at standalone level** — part wage code implemented from **December 2025**, part deliberate over-hiring ("we are building the staff cost **ahead of the curve**"). Permanent headcount +~4,000 (highest ever) while contractual headcount rose only ~2,200 vs a ~10,000 three-year average — the contractual gap is mechanization/productivity, plus a 31-March point-in-time BRSR reading.
> 3. **Total debt of INR2,267 cr is not comparable to prior "net debt"** — it includes the Ind AS 116 lease liability. Real borrowing is **INR965 cr**.
> 4. **FY26's 85 store adds flatter the base twice over**: properties readied faster than planned so openings were pulled into Q4 (analyst put ~60 stores in Q4, unrefuted), meaning FY26 revenue captured almost none of them — but FY27 gets a full-year kicker while FY27 *additions* mechanically normalise toward ~75.
> 5. **Inventory days rose to 33.2 on new warehouse openings**, not on slow-moving stock.
> 6. **AOV of ~INR1,600 is an analyst figure** (Nihal Jham, HSBC) that management worked with but never confirmed — treat as approximate.
guidance (critical — verify next quarter:
DMart is structurally guidance-shy; what follows is everything that was actually committed, and the refusals are noted.

- **Store additions:** "internally, our benchmarks will remain that we should be **opening around 15% of our store base** as the number that we want to increase annually" — with the honest caveat that real estate means "some years this could be a few percentages higher and some it could be a few percentages lower." On a ~500 base this is a **~75-store run-rate**. Asked twice whether it could be 20% again, or 100–150 stores: **no**, 15% is the working number "at least in the foreseeable future."
- **Like-for-like growth:** SSSG to hold **"around the current trend"**, explicitly clarified twice as **last financial year's level (8.1%)**, not last quarter's. On the 7.5–8% band beyond FY27: "in the coming financial year, we see that this is something which is **possible for us to deliver**." Metro SSSG explicitly will **not** return to double digits "all things being constant."
- **Margin:** **"15% kind of a gross margin and let's say around a 5% kind of a net margin should be the North Star for this business even in the future."** No material downside risk to net margin flagged. Equally, **no upside** — any sourcing/productivity gain inside the 14–15% band gets **passed to customers**.
- **Category mix:** General merchandise & apparel to stay at **22–23%** of sales; explicitly **no intent** to push it back to historical levels.
- **Capex / funding:** FY26 capex was **"upwards of INR4,000 cr"** and "with the increasing store count that we want to pursue, we will need some capex." Borrowing **may reach ~INR2,000 cr by end-FY27** (INR1,000 cr NCD alongside existing CP), then — the big one — **"in next two-three years, the existing stores will generate enough capital for us to not keep on borrowing anymore."**
- **DMart Ready:** prove a **sustainable, profitable** model in **11 cities** with **sub-6-hour delivery**, then expand. AEL **losses "reduced significantly"**; efficiency gains to show **in FY27 and onwards** (Vikram Dasu: "That's right"). **No** instant/10-minute delivery — "We are not looking at that as an option." **No** plan to merge AEL into the store business.
- **Tech/ERP overhaul:** margin trade-off "will be very marginal… nothing we would need to flag."
- **Explicitly refused to disclose:** lease-vs-owned store economics, DMart Ready AOV / transaction growth / same-PIN-code growth ("Cannot say. That's a good attempt."), city-level productivity variance, store-level P&L, and the land value split between operating and pipeline stores.
store pipeline (order-book substitute):
There is no order book; the forward-visibility asset is the **land bank and project execution pipeline**, and management quantified it: **"we are sitting on a project execution pipeline of next two to three years of stores that we will open."** Land converts to store in **2–3 years** depending on configuration (double-basement + multi-storey is slow, ground-floor is fast), so FY26's openings largely reflect FY23–FY24 land buys. Land is capitalised at registration, which is why the balance-sheet land number cannot be read as operating assets.

The **lease option is now formally open** as a pipeline accelerant: **68 of the 500+ stores are on long leases**, of which **15 were added in FY26 alone** (i.e. 53 accumulated over all prior years — the mix is clearly shifting). Asked whether lease share must rise: "Possibly it would, because there will be certain cities that we'd want to go to where we might have to go for the lease option" — **NCR named specifically**. There is no target lease percentage. Smaller boxes are also now acceptable: "there is no requirement that we need to necessarily have a 40,000-plus square foot store."

Bottleneck, stated plainly: it is **not** capital and **not** people ("We have increased manpower… manpower is not a constraint"). It is **clean land parcels + regulatory permissions + the 2–3 year build cycle**. Property-conversion rates from shortlist to purchase "have more or less remained steady." Expansion follows the **70:30 rule** — 70% densification in existing states, 30% new states — and FY27's priority is **building density in the five states entered in FY26**.
segment / subsidiary detail:
- **ASL (stores)** — the engine. Category mix "remained pretty steady": slight dip in non-food, marginal increase in food, garments/apparel stable. Management refused to read anything into the food/non-food shift, attributing it to category-level inflation and geographic mix, and **explicitly rejected the GST-rate-cut explanation** an analyst offered.
- **AEL / DMart Ready** — the story of the call. Footprint **cut from 18 to 11 cities**; the 7 exited cities delivered "very minimal" contribution and had **capacity utilisation, throughput and order density below expectation**. Three fixes underway: online-tailored **assortment**, **sub-6-hour** slotted delivery, better **UX**. The model is deliberately **delivery-first — pickup points "take a backseat"** (165 remain). Assortment is predominantly FMCG food and non-food with far less general merchandise than stores, so **structurally lower gross margin**, and management said it "probably will never match" store levels — the profit path is operational efficiency, not mix. **Ad/marketplace monetisation of the app is untouched and explicitly acknowledged as an unpulled lever.** Minimum order value is **variable by city**.
- **Align Retail** (grocery packing) — sales +16.5%, PAT +24%. Quietly the highest-quality growth in the group.
- **Avenue Food Plaza** (ready-food adjacent to each store) — sales **+35.5%**, now at **9% PAT margin** after a loss last year on expansion. Fastest-growing entity in the group off a small base.
growth verticals / optionality:
- **Geographic whitespace** is the entire thesis. Management's repeated framing: total organised trade — modern retail + e-commerce + quick commerce combined — is still only **"early teens"** as a share of Indian retail. Growth = "being available in more states, more cities, more markets."
- **Tier-1/Tier-2 stores are outgrowing the company average** (confirmed directly: "the SSG in those stores would be much better than your company average?" — "Yes"), with lower property and operating costs, though lower initial productivity that "gradually picks up." Brand strength in a state materially accelerates ramp-up in that state's smaller towns.
- **Fresh is an option, not a plan.** Pilots with fresh fruit in Mumbai are "giving some strong results," but "is there a plan to have a full-fledged fresh portfolio in DMart stores at this point of time? **No**." This matters because fresh is roughly the half of the retail TAM DMart does not address.
- **Technology & data stack modernisation** — the new CEO's flagship priority, spanning "our ERP system to all our operations," to run tighter operations across categories, store ops and supply chain.
- **Management bandwidth build** — hiring ahead of the curve across senior and store levels plus new technology talent, explicitly to support "a much bigger footprint."
- **Inorganic / partnership entry into quick commerce** — asked directly, Asawa did not deny it: "this is something that we cannot discuss here on this call. I'd leave this to more discussion **at the board level**." That is a materially softer answer than the flat "no" given to instant delivery.
6a. moat & competitive position:
- **The build-and-own real-estate model is named as the moat** — "This being our moat is what we would not want to give up," given as the *reason* store growth is capped at 15%. DMart is deliberately accepting slower expansion to preserve owned-asset cost structure.
- **EDLP through everyday-low-cost operations** — the CEO's framing: it "isn't just a strategy, but it also has become its moat and will continue to protect us for years to come."
- **The 14–15% gross margin itself is claimed as the moat** — Niladri Deb: "our healthy gross margin is in the range of 14% to 15%, which keeps us very, very competitive, and **that's the moat that we look at**." A retailer treating a *ceiling* on margin as the moat is the clearest possible statement that value is passed through.
- **Vendor position** — "in many cases, for example, we are the **number one retailer for them** as an individual entity"; key vendors met twice in the year; FMCG partners are "doubling down," not diverting attention to quick commerce.
- **Basket-level value, not SKU-level price** — the defence against pricing-parity claims: on an INR5,000 basket the customer should save INR1,500–2,000; on the ~INR1,600 average bill, savings are "significantly more than 10%."
- **20-20-20 private-label discipline** — at least **20% price advantage** to the customer, at least **20% higher margin** than the benchmark, at least **20% volume share**. Unchanged under the new CEO. India remains "a very brand-conscious market" and "an MRP-driven market" where comparisons are easy, so private label is a value tool, not a margin tool. (Note: the 20-20-20 count excludes garments, general merchandise and DMart Grocery.) The observed rise in private-label shelf space is "driven more by customer choice" — "no such conscious effort."
margins & cost dynamics:
Gross margin rose just **16 bps** with no mix change — described as simply "rational for the margins that we make on the business." Everything below gross margin is where FY26 went: **employee cost +27bps of sales (+33% in absolute standalone terms)**, offset only partly by other expenses −9bps, leaving EBITDA flat at ~7.85% and dragging PBT/PAT down 26/25bps. The employee build is explicitly **pre-investment** — "we are building the organization for a very large organization size… building the staff cost **ahead of the curve**" — and management would not say the build is finished ("Whether this is the end or not, very difficult to say").

The margin philosophy is the important part, and it is a hard ceiling: **"We do not want to make margins which are beyond, let's say, reasonable levels"** — any sourcing or productivity gain inside 14–15% goes back to the customer. Asked whether competition had forced deeper discounting that masked a better underlying gross margin, Asawa neither confirmed nor denied a number but said any impact was "business as usual" and offset by efficiencies.

At store level, management does **not** manage margin: "We don't look at a store level margin in that much detail, and this is not a metric that we chase with our store teams." Wage-code and general inflation are being absorbed by throughput growth. On leases, Niladri Deb was precise: **Ind AS 116 finance and depreciation costs sit below EBITDA, so PBT is the fair indicator** of lease impact — but at 15 of 85 additions, "not a very big number to distort the P&L widely."

At AEL, cost inflation was severe and network-driven: **contract labour +24%, transport +34%** — the direct consequence of running deliveries across cities with insufficient order density, and the reason for the 11-city consolidation.
capex / expansion (watch slippage):
- **FY26 capex "upwards of INR4,000 cr"** against CFO of INR4,168 cr — i.e. the store programme now consumes essentially all operating cash.
- **FY27 plan:** ~15% of base ≈ **75 stores**; open to a couple of percentage points either way; open to **long-term leases** and to **sub-40,000 sq ft boxes** where the market warrants.
- **Retail area 20.6 mn sq ft** at Mar-26 is the base to track; revenue per sq ft was flat at **INR33,422**, so incremental revenue should track incremental area almost linearly *after* the 1–2 year ramp.
- **Funding:** CP ~INR800 cr + **INR1,000 cr NCD approved** → borrowing may reach **~INR2,000 cr by end-FY27**. The NCD is a **cost-of-debt and interest-rate-risk** play, not a liquidity need: "if you go to the CP market every quarter, you run an interest rate risk."
- **Slippage risk is real but two-sided** — FY26 *over*-delivered because properties readied early and were pushed into Q4. The same mechanic can reverse.
- **Watch:** whether FY27 store adds land at 75 or slip toward 60; whether lease share of adds rises above FY26's 15/85 (18%); whether borrowing stops at INR2,000 cr.
capital allocation:
The honest disclosure of the call came from Niladri Deb: **"we did a fundraise in 2020… promoter dilution of close to half a billion dollars. That money is over now, and hence we are doing a fundraise."** DMart is, for the first time in its listed life, funding expansion with debt because RoNW (13.5%) and ROCE (17.1%) no longer generate enough internal accrual to fund a growing store programme — and both slipped YoY.

The counter-argument management offered: store cost in non-metros is far below metros, and the existing 500-store base should self-fund expansion **within two to three years**. That is the single most checkable capital-allocation claim on the call. An analyst pushed correctly that unless the return profile improves, external capital becomes permanent — management did not rebut the logic, only the timeline.

Everything else is store capex. No dividend, no buyback, no equity issuance discussed. risks & watch-items:
- **Metro same-store growth is structurally impaired, and management said so.** Cause is a stack: store **maturity/saturation** at high throughput, **deliberate self-cannibalisation** (opening a second store nearby to relieve pressure), and **quick commerce**. On QC's drag: "I'm suspecting that that's **not going to change over the next few years**."
- **Quick-commerce competitive intensity is rising, not plateauing** — Amazon Now and Flipkart Minutes have entered, with analysts citing a 2,000-store Flipkart build-out and ~6,000 dark stores in India. Management's answer was market-size ("early teens" organised share), not a competitive counter-move, and admitted it has done **no work and holds no view** on QC adoption beyond the top 10–12 cities.
- **Pricing-parity erosion.** Analysts report anecdotal price parity with QC platforms online. Management's rebuttal is basket-level saving, but conceded it does not have the like-for-like basket-value trend "right away" and would try to provide it — an evidence gap on the core proposition.
- **Wage code (from Dec-2025) + general wage inflation** is now permanently in the cost base, with no statement that the capability build is complete.
- **Rising leverage with slipping returns** — RoNW 13.5% and ROCE 17.1% both down; borrowing heading to ~INR2,000 cr. If the "self-funding in 2–3 years" claim slips, the equity story changes materially.
- **AEL execution risk** — INR307 cr loss, cost lines inflating 24–34%, and losses that *grew with expansion*. The 11-city model is unproven; a second retreat would be far more damaging than the first.

- **Fresh absence** — competitors (QC platforms, Star Bazaar) position fresh-first; DMart addresses roughly half the retail TAM and has no fresh plan.

management quality / tone:
Unusually candid for a first call. On DMart Ready he was blunt: **"let me be very transparent here… as we've tried to expand into more and more cities, the number of customers acquired were larger, but our losses also grew quite significantly."** That is an admission of a failed expansion, volunteered.

The refusals were consistent and unapologetic rather than evasive — lease economics, DMart Ready AOV and PIN-code growth ("Cannot say. That's a good attempt."), city productivity variance, land-value splits. Notably, an internal correction was made in real time (65 → 68 lease stores) rather than left standing. Vikram Dasu answered the AEL cost question with the specific inflation numbers rather than deflecting.

Where the tone was weakest: the quick-commerce answers were repetitive and market-size-based ("organised trade is in early teens") across at least six questioners, and management admitted it has done no consumer research on switching behaviour and has no view on QC adoption in smaller cities. non-obvious takeaways:
- **The 15% benchmark is a downgrade dressed as clarity.** FY26 delivered ~20% store growth (85 adds). Anchoring publicly at 15% resets expectations *down* while sounding like new transparency. And because ~60 of the 85 opened in Q4 FY26, FY27 revenue inherits a full-year kicker from stores that contributed almost nothing to FY26 — so FY27 revenue growth can look fine even as *store adds* decelerate. The optics and the run-rate will diverge.
- **Gross margin is a declared ceiling, not a lever.** Management calls 14–15% "the moat" and commits to passing sourcing gains to customers. Combined with flat revenue per sq ft, that means earnings growth is arithmetically **area × ramp**, with zero contribution from mix, price or private label. Any cost step-up (as with the 33% wage bill) drops straight through to PBT with nothing to offset it. That is a very specific and testable earnings model.
- **DMart has quietly become a leveraged compounder.** "That money is over now" — the 2020 promoter-dilution proceeds are spent, capex now exceeds nothing less than the entire operating cash flow, and borrowing is heading to ~INR2,000 cr. The 2–3-year self-funding promise is the load-bearing assumption in the whole story; if store adds accelerate as promised, self-funding gets *harder*, not easier — the two commitments are in tension.
- **Refusing to collect offline customer data is now a strategic constraint, not just a philosophy.** The new CEO's stated priority is a data and tech overhaul — but he explicitly ring-fenced it away from the customer: data modernisation covers categories, store operations and supply chain, while the store checkout stays anonymous "because one of the values this organization is built around is simplicity." So DMart cannot build personalisation, loyalty or win-back mechanics against QC in stores. Its only customer-identified asset is DMart Ready — the loss-making 11-city business.
- **Self-cannibalisation is now an admitted part of the SSSG number.** Management opens a second store near a saturated one to relieve throughput pressure, "which of course impacts the SSSG." So reported LFL is depressed partly *by DMart's own capex* — a bear on SSSG is partly a bull on area growth, and the two metrics must be read together, never separately.
- **The AEL retreat may be a gift to the quick-commerce incumbents.** Seven cities were vacated because order density was too low — exactly the density problem QC players solve with dark-store scale. DMart has effectively conceded those markets online while its store base keeps expanding into them.
- **The unpulled monetisation lever was named on the record.** "We don't really monetize our app and site experiences, but **that's a big lever at any point in time we can pull**." AEL's path to profitability therefore has an undisclosed ad-revenue option on top of the efficiency plan.
- **The inorganic QC door was left ajar.** Asawa flatly refused instant delivery as an operating model, but on inorganic opportunities or strategic partnerships in quick commerce he deferred to "the board level" — a materially different answer, and the single most interesting non-denial on the call.
- **Avenue Food Plaza is the group's quiet compounder** — +35.5% growth at 9% PAT margin, better than the core retail business's net margin, on adjacencies to existing stores requiring near-zero incremental real estate. It is never discussed as a strategy.

capital allocation:
The honest disclosure of the call came from Niladri Deb: **"we did a fundraise in 2020… promoter dilution of close to half a billion dollars. That money is over now, and hence we are doing a fundraise."** DMart is, for the first time in its listed life, funding expansion with debt because RoNW (13.5%) and ROCE (17.1%) no longer generate enough internal accrual to fund a growing store programme — and both slipped YoY.

The counter-argument management offered: store cost in non-metros is far below metros, and the existing 500-store base should self-fund expansion **within two to three years**. That is the single most checkable capital-allocation claim on the call. An analyst pushed correctly that unless the return profile improves, external capital becomes permanent — management did not rebut the logic, only the timeline.

Everything else is store capex. No dividend, no buyback, no equity issuance discussed. Payables are deliberately kept at **7.2 days** — "continuing our strategy of paying vendors quickly," which is a conscious decision to fund the vendor rather than the balance sheet, and is part of the vendor-relationship moat.
risks & watch-items:
- **Metro same-store growth is structurally impaired, and management said so.** Cause is a stack: store **maturity/saturation** at high throughput, **deliberate self-cannibalisation** (opening a second store nearby to relieve pressure), and **quick commerce**. On QC's drag: "I'm suspecting that that's **not going to change over the next few years**."
- **Quick-commerce competitive intensity is rising, not plateauing** — Amazon Now and Flipkart Minutes have entered, with analysts citing a 2,000-store Flipkart build-out and ~6,000 dark stores in India. Management's answer was market-size ("early teens" organised share), not a competitive counter-move, and admitted it has done **no work and holds no view** on QC adoption beyond the top 10–12 cities.
- **Pricing-parity erosion.** Analysts report anecdotal price parity with QC platforms online. Management's rebuttal is basket-level saving, but conceded it does not have the like-for-like basket-value trend "right away" and would try to provide it — an evidence gap on the core proposition.
- **Wage code (from Dec-2025) + general wage inflation** is now permanently in the cost base, with no statement that the capability build is complete.
- **Rising leverage with slipping returns** — RoNW 13.5% and ROCE 17.1% both down; borrowing heading to ~INR2,000 cr. If the "self-funding in 2–3 years" claim slips, the equity story changes materially.
- **AEL execution risk** — INR307 cr loss, cost lines inflating 24–34%, and losses that *grew with expansion*. The 11-city model is unproven; a second retreat would be far more damaging than the first.
- **No offline customer data, by choice** — DMart deliberately does not collect store customer data (simplicity/checkout speed), and has run **no consumer study** on customers shifting to QC. It therefore cannot answer whether defectors are visiting less often or buying smaller baskets. That is a real blind spot against data-native competitors.
- **Fresh absence** — competitors (QC platforms, Star Bazaar) position fresh-first; DMart addresses roughly half the retail TAM and has no fresh plan.
- **Real estate is the hard constraint on the entire growth algorithm**, and it is not something capital or headcount can fix.
- **New CEO transition risk** — leadership changes flagged as coming "as superannuation happens or some exits happen," to be announced as they occur.
management quality / tone:
Unusually candid for a first call. Asawa was direct where DMart has historically been vague — he **deliberately put a number (15%) on store growth** ("this time I wanted to be a bit deliberate"), openly said FY26's 85 stores were an *upside surprise* driven by properties readying early rather than a new run-rate, and conceded metro SSSG will not recover. On DMart Ready he was blunt: **"let me be very transparent here… as we've tried to expand into more and more cities, the number of customers acquired were larger, but our losses also grew quite significantly."** That is an admission of a failed expansion, volunteered.

The refusals were consistent and unapologetic rather than evasive — lease economics, DMart Ready AOV and PIN-code growth ("Cannot say. That's a good attempt."), city productivity variance, land-value splits. Notably, an internal correction was made in real time (65 → 68 lease stores) rather than left standing. Vikram Dasu answered the AEL cost question with the specific inflation numbers rather than deflecting.

Where the tone was weakest: the quick-commerce answers were repetitive and market-size-based ("organised trade is in early teens") across at least six questioners, and management admitted it has done no consumer research on switching behaviour and has no view on QC adoption in smaller cities. That is a genuine analytical gap, not just a disclosure choice. The inorganic-QC question was parked at "board level" rather than refused — the one place the door was left open.
non-obvious takeaways:
- **The 15% benchmark is a downgrade dressed as clarity.** FY26 delivered ~20% store growth (85 adds). Anchoring publicly at 15% resets expectations *down* while sounding like new transparency. And because ~60 of the 85 opened in Q4 FY26, FY27 revenue inherits a full-year kicker from stores that contributed almost nothing to FY26 — so FY27 revenue growth can look fine even as *store adds* decelerate. The optics and the run-rate will diverge.
- **Gross margin is a declared ceiling, not a lever.** Management calls 14–15% "the moat" and commits to passing sourcing gains to customers. Combined with flat revenue per sq ft, that means earnings growth is arithmetically **area × ramp**, with zero contribution from mix, price or private label. Any cost step-up (as with the 33% wage bill) drops straight through to PBT with nothing to offset it. That is a very specific and testable earnings model.
- **DMart has quietly become a leveraged compounder.** "That money is over now" — the 2020 promoter-dilution proceeds are spent, capex now exceeds nothing less than the entire operating cash flow, and borrowing is heading to ~INR2,000 cr. The 2–3-year self-funding promise is the load-bearing assumption in the whole story; if store adds accelerate as promised, self-funding gets *harder*, not easier — the two commitments are in tension.
- **Refusing to collect offline customer data is now a strategic constraint, not just a philosophy.** The new CEO's stated priority is a data and tech overhaul — but he explicitly ring-fenced it away from the customer: data modernisation covers categories, store operations and supply chain, while the store checkout stays anonymous "because one of the values this organization is built around is simplicity." So DMart cannot build personalisation, loyalty or win-back mechanics against QC in stores. Its only customer-identified asset is DMart Ready — the loss-making 11-city business.
- **Self-cannibalisation is now an admitted part of the SSSG number.** Management opens a second store near a saturated one to relieve throughput pressure, "which of course impacts the SSSG." So reported LFL is depressed partly *by DMart's own capex* — a bear on SSSG is partly a bull on area growth, and the two metrics must be read together, never separately.
- **The AEL retreat may be a gift to the quick-commerce incumbents.** Seven cities were vacated because order density was too low — exactly the density problem QC players solve with dark-store scale. DMart has effectively conceded those markets online while its store base keeps expanding into them.
- **The unpulled monetisation lever was named on the record.** "We don't really monetize our app and site experiences, but **that's a big lever at any point in time we can pull**." AEL's path to profitability therefore has an undisclosed ad-revenue option on top of the efficiency plan.
- **The inorganic QC door was left ajar.** Asawa flatly refused instant delivery as an operating model, but on inorganic opportunities or strategic partnerships in quick commerce he deferred to "the board level" — a materially different answer, and the single most interesting non-denial on the call.
- **Avenue Food Plaza is the group's quiet compounder** — +35.5% growth at 9% PAT margin, better than the core retail business's net margin, on adjacencies to existing stores requiring near-zero incremental real estate. It is never discussed as a strategy.

themes.title: Quick-commerce, omnichannel & retail expansion
themes.need: Quick-commerce and value retail are the structural growth engine, and Q1FY27 rewrote the unit-economics model. ETERNAL raised Blinkit's steady-state margin from a 5-6% range to ~6% and set a first-ever 4% GAAP EBIT margin target (after ESOP and depreciation) while capex per store went from INR 1cr to INR 2.5cr (+150%) with NOV/store/day up only 60% and net working capital improving 18 to 14 days - so margin can now drift DOWN while ROCE improves. Growth also decoupled from spend: Blinkit orders +21% QoQ with MTUs above 30mn achieved on LOWER marketing spend and fewer store adds, and management called Q1 the peak of competitive intensity to date. VMM did INR 3,727cr (+18.7%) on 10% SSSG with gross margin up to 28.7% driven by lower promotional spend rather than price hikes, validated a small-format store at the same revenue/sq ft and 'pretty much the same' ROCE as large format (a ~3,000-store national opportunity), and found 20% of its quick-commerce customers had never shopped a Vishal store. SHOPERSTOP swung PAT positive (+INR 5cr vs -INR 4cr) and raised FY27 LFL guidance from 5% to ~6%; ARVINDFASN lifted gross margin 90bps to 56.7% on full-price sell-through with direct channels now 62% of sales; MEESHO cut cost per delivered order ~INR 1 QoQ despite the May fuel hike. DMART/V2RETAIL/PATELRMART on value retail; TRENT-tier branded retail via ABFRL/METROBRAND/BATAINDIA/REDTAPE.
themes.driver: Blinkit dark-store rollout at the new INR 2.5cr/store capex against the 4% GAAP EBIT target; VMM small-format expansion; festive/quick-commerce GMV. Watch ARVINDFASN's SS27 sourcing lock (next 45-60 days) - if war-inflated input costs hold, apparel pricing corrects.

hero.oneLiner: Avenue Supermarts Limited (DMart) is a national value-retailing supermarket chain built on the Everyday Low Cost / Everyday Low Price (EDLC/EDLP) principle.
hero.industry: Retail / Value Grocery & Hypermarkets — EDLP brick-and-mortar + grocery e-commerce

one_liner.title: One Liner (RHP)
one_liner.body: Avenue Supermarts Limited (DMart) is a national value-retailing supermarket chain built on the Everyday Low Cost / Everyday Low Price (EDLC/EDLP) principle.

business_model.title: What they do
business_model.body: DMart is a national supermarket chain focused on value-retailing, offering a wide range of products across the Foods, Non-Foods (FMCG) and General Merchandise & Apparel categories. Since its first store in Mumbai in 2002 it has grown to 500 stores with 20.58 million sq. ft. of retail business area across 15 states, 1 union territory and NCR, supported by a network of distribution centres and packing centres. Its store offerings aim to provide one-stop shop convenience for customers' everyday shopping needs in a modern ambience with the feel of a large retail mall.

group_structure.title: Group structure (profile)
group_structure.body:
- Align Retail Trades Private Limited (ARTPL) — subsidiary: Wholly owned subsidiary incorporated on 22nd September, 2006; engaged in the business of packing and selling of grocery products, spices, dry fruits, etc.
- Avenue Food Plaza Private Limited (AFPPL) — subsidiary: Wholly owned subsidiary incorporated on 8th June, 2004; engaged in the business of operating food outlets at DMart stores.
- Avenue E-Commerce Limited (AEL) — subsidiary: Subsidiary incorporated on 11th November, 2014; engaged in online and multi-channel grocery retail under the brand name DMart Ready, serving customers through its mobile app and website www.dmart.in. Completed 9 years in e-commerce in January 2026 and strengthened its Home Delivery business; service footprint of 18 cities including the Mumbai Metropolitan Region. Also the counterparty to the proposed material related party transaction for sale of goods by the Company.

segment_detail.title: Segment / subsidiary detail
segment_detail.body:
- **ASL (stores)** — the engine. Category mix "remained pretty steady": slight dip in non-food, marginal increase in food, garments/apparel stable. Management refused to read anything into the food/non-food shift, attributing it to category-level inflation and geographic mix, and **explicitly rejected the GST-rate-cut explanation** an analyst offered.
- **AEL / DMart Ready** — the story of the call. Footprint **cut from 18 to 11 cities**; the 7 exited cities delivered "very minimal" contribution and had **capacity utilisation, throughput and order density below expectation**. Three fixes underway: online-tailored **assortment**, **sub-6-hour** slotted delivery, better **UX**. The model is deliberately **delivery-first — pickup points "take a backseat"** (165 remain). Assortment is predominantly FMCG food and non-food with far less general merchandise than stores, so **structurally lower gross margin**, and management said it "probably will never match" store levels — the profit path is operational efficiency, not mix. **Ad/marketplace monetisation of the app is untouched and explicitly acknowledged as an unpulled lever.** Minimum order value is **variable by city**.
- **Align Retail** (grocery packing) — sales +16.5%, PAT +24%. Quietly the highest-quality growth in the group.
- **Avenue Food Plaza** (ready-food adjacent to each store) — sales **+35.5%**, now at **9% PAT margin** after a loss last year on expansion. Fastest-growing entity in the group off a small base.

end_markets.title: End Markets (RHP)
end_markets.body:
- India - domestic value retail; no stated international presence
- Maharashtra, Gujarat, Telangana, Andhra Pradesh, Karnataka, Madhya Pradesh, Tamil Nadu, Rajasthan, Punjab, NCR, Chhattisgarh, Uttar Pradesh, Uttarakhand, Goa, Orissa, Haryana and Daman
- Everyday value retail shoppers seeking one-stop convenience for daily shopping needs

order_book.title: Store pipeline (order-book substitute)
order_book.body:
There is no order book; the forward-visibility asset is the **land bank and project execution pipeline**, and management quantified it: **"we are sitting on a project execution pipeline of next two to three years of stores that we will open."** Land converts to store in **2–3 years** depending on configuration (double-basement + multi-storey is slow, ground-floor is fast), so FY26's openings largely reflect FY23–FY24 land buys. Land is capitalised at registration, which is why the balance-sheet land number cannot be read as operating assets.

The **lease option is now formally open** as a pipeline accelerant: **68 of the 500+ stores are on long leases**, of which **15 were added in FY26 alone** (i.e. 53 accumulated over all prior years — the mix is clearly shifting). Asked whether lease share must rise: "Possibly it would, because there will be certain cities that we'd want to go to where we might have to go for the lease option" — **NCR named specifically**. There is no target lease percentage. Smaller boxes are also now acceptable: "there is no requirement that we need to necessarily have a 40,000-plus square foot store."

Bottleneck, stated plainly: it is **not** capital and **not** people ("We have increased manpower… manpower is not a constraint"). It is **clean land parcels + regulatory permissions + the 2–3 year build cycle**. Property-conversion rates from shortlist to purchase "have more or less remained steady." Expansion follows the **70:30 rule** — 70% densification in existing states, 30% new states — and FY27's priority is **building density in the five states entered in FY26**.

guidance.title: Guidance (CRITICAL — verify next quarter)
guidance.body:
DMart is structurally guidance-shy; what follows is everything that was actually committed, and the refusals are noted.

- **Store additions:** "internally, our benchmarks will remain that we should be **opening around 15% of our store base** as the number that we want to increase annually" — with the honest caveat that real estate means "some years this could be a few percentages higher and some it could be a few percentages lower." On a ~500 base this is a **~75-store run-rate**. Asked twice whether it could be 20% again, or 100–150 stores: **no**, 15% is the working number "at least in the foreseeable future."
- **Like-for-like growth:** SSSG to hold **"around the current trend"**, explicitly clarified twice as **last financial year's level (8.1%)**, not last quarter's. On the 7.5–8% band beyond FY27: "in the coming financial year, we see that this is something which is **possible for us to deliver**." Metro SSSG explicitly will **not** return to double digits "all things being constant."
- **Margin:** **"15% kind of a gross margin and let's say around a 5% kind of a net margin should be the North Star for this business even in the future."** No material downside risk to net margin flagged. Equally, **no upside** — any sourcing/productivity gain inside the 14–15% band gets **passed to customers**.
- **Category mix:** General merchandise & apparel to stay at **22–23%** of sales; explicitly **no intent** to push it back to historical levels.
- **Capex / funding:** FY26 capex was **"upwards of INR4,000 cr"** and "with the increasing store count that we want to pursue, we will need some capex." Borrowing **may reach ~INR2,000 cr by end-FY27** (INR1,000 cr NCD alongside existing CP), then — the big one — **"in next two-three years, the existing stores will generate enough capital for us to not keep on borrowing anymore."**
- **DMart Ready:** prove a **sustainable, profitable** model in **11 cities** with **sub-6-hour delivery**, then expand. AEL **losses "reduced significantly"**; efficiency gains to show **in FY27 and onwards** (Vikram Dasu: "That's right"). **No** instant/10-minute delivery — "We are not looking at that as an option." **No** plan to merge AEL into the store business.
- **Tech/ERP overhaul:** margin trade-off "will be very marginal… nothing we would need to flag."
- **Explicitly refused to disclose:** lease-vs-owned store economics, DMart Ready AOV / transaction growth / same-PIN-code growth ("Cannot say. That's a good attempt."), city-level productivity variance, store-level P&L, and the land value split between operating and pipeline stores.

growth_optionality.title: Growth verticals / optionality
growth_optionality.body:
- **Geographic whitespace** is the entire thesis. Management's repeated framing: total organised trade — modern retail + e-commerce + quick commerce combined — is still only **"early teens"** as a share of Indian retail. Growth = "being available in more states, more cities, more markets."
- **Tier-1/Tier-2 stores are outgrowing the company average** (confirmed directly: "the SSG in those stores would be much better than your company average?" — "Yes"), with lower property and operating costs, though lower initial productivity that "gradually picks up." Brand strength in a state materially accelerates ramp-up in that state's smaller towns.
- **Fresh is an option, not a plan.** Pilots with fresh fruit in Mumbai are "giving some strong results," but "is there a plan to have a full-fledged fresh portfolio in DMart stores at this point of time? **No**." This matters because fresh is roughly the half of the retail TAM DMart does not address.
- **Technology & data stack modernisation** — the new CEO's flagship priority, spanning "our ERP system to all our operations," to run tighter operations across categories, store ops and supply chain.
- **Management bandwidth build** — hiring ahead of the curve across senior and store levels plus new technology talent, explicitly to support "a much bigger footprint."
- **Inorganic / partnership entry into quick commerce** — asked directly, Asawa did not deny it: "this is something that we cannot discuss here on this call. I'd leave this to more discussion **at the board level**." That is a materially softer answer than the flat "no" given to instant delivery.

demand_drivers.title: Demand & outlook drivers
demand_drivers.body:
- The Indian economy grew by an estimated 7.7% in FY 2025-26 versus 7.1% in the previous year, with domestic consumption resilience acting as a strategic buffer against external shocks
- GDP growth is expected at 7.1% in fiscal 2027 (Crisil Research), with benign inflation and increased public spending allocations likely to provide economic stability
- Ongoing geopolitical instability and volatile commodity prices continue to weigh on the economy
- Overall retail industry estimated to have grown at ~10% to INR 112 trillion in FY 2025-26; organised retail grew 15% to INR 15 trillion (~13% of overall retail) and E-retail 16% to INR 5.5 trillion (~4.9%)
- Food and grocery accounts for about 32% (in value terms) of the organised retail industry as of FY 2025-26
- Retail industry expected to grow at a CAGR of 9.7-10.4% between 2025 and 2030 (CRISIL Research)
- Consumption revival coupled with economic growth is likely to boost consumer sentiment and drive discretionary spending
- Total bill cuts rose to 39.8 crore in FY 2025-26 from 35.3 crore in FY 2024-25
- Annualised revenue from sales per retail business area sq. ft. was INR 33,422 in FY 2025-26 versus INR 33,896 in FY 2024-25
- Store network and retail business area continued to grow steadily, with retail business area at 20.6 million sq. ft. in FY 2025-26 versus 17.2 million sq. ft. in FY 2024-25
- Headcount of 20,994 permanent employees and 75,577 contractual employees at the end of FY 2025-26 supports the store and distribution-centre network

margins.title: Margins & cost dynamics
margins.body:
Gross margin rose just **16 bps** with no mix change — described as simply "rational for the margins that we make on the business." Everything below gross margin is where FY26 went: **employee cost +27bps of sales (+33% in absolute standalone terms)**, offset only partly by other expenses −9bps, leaving EBITDA flat at ~7.85% and dragging PBT/PAT down 26/25bps. The employee build is explicitly **pre-investment** — "we are building the organization for a very large organization size… building the staff cost **ahead of the curve**" — and management would not say the build is finished ("Whether this is the end or not, very difficult to say").

The margin philosophy is the important part, and it is a hard ceiling: **"We do not want to make margins which are beyond, let's say, reasonable levels"** — any sourcing or productivity gain inside 14–15% goes back to the customer. Asked whether competition had forced deeper discounting that masked a better underlying gross margin, Asawa neither confirmed nor denied a number but said any impact was "business as usual" and offset by efficiencies.

At store level, management does **not** manage margin: "We don't look at a store level margin in that much detail, and this is not a metric that we chase with our store teams." Wage-code and general inflation are being absorbed by throughput growth. On leases, Niladri Deb was precise: **Ind AS 116 finance and depreciation costs sit below EBITDA, so PBT is the fair indicator** of lease impact — but at 15 of 85 additions, "not a very big number to distort the P&L widely."

At AEL, cost inflation was severe and network-driven: **contract labour +24%, transport +34%** — the direct consequence of running deliveries across cities with insufficient order density, and the reason for the 11-city consolidation.

capital_allocation.title: Capital allocation
capital_allocation.body:
The honest disclosure of the call came from Niladri Deb: **"we did a fundraise in 2020… promoter dilution of close to half a billion dollars. That money is over now, and hence we are doing a fundraise."** DMart is, for the first time in its listed life, funding expansion with debt because RoNW (13.5%) and ROCE (17.1%) no longer generate enough internal accrual to fund a growing store programme — and both slipped YoY.

The counter-argument management offered: store cost in non-metros is far below metros, and the existing 500-store base should self-fund expansion **within two to three years**. That is the single most checkable capital-allocation claim on the call. An analyst pushed correctly that unless the return profile improves, external capital becomes permanent — management did not rebut the logic, only the timeline.

Everything else is store capex. No dividend, no buyback, no equity issuance discussed. Payables are deliberately kept at **7.2 days** — "continuing our strategy of paying vendors quickly," which is a conscious decision to fund the vendor rather than the balance sheet, and is part of the vendor-relationship moat.

capex_expansion.title: Capex & expansion plans
capex_expansion.body: Expansion in FY 2025-26 was entirely store-network led: the Company added 85 new stores during the year, taking the total to 500 stores as of 31st March, 2026 across 15 states, 1 union territory and NCR, with retail business area of 20.58 million sq. ft. (up from 17.2 million sq. ft. in FY 2024-25). The store footprint is spread across Maharashtra (128), Gujarat (75), Karnataka (50), Telangana (48), Andhra Pradesh (47), Tamil Nadu (35), Madhya Pradesh (29), Rajasthan (28), Punjab (24), NCR (20), Chhattisgarh (8), Uttar Pradesh (3), and one store each in Uttarakhand, Goa, Orissa, Haryana and Daman. Store operations are supported by a back-end network of 84 distribution centres and 12 packing centres as of 31st March, 2026. The routed text sets out no forward store-addition target, no rupee capex plan and no dated project commissioning schedule; instead it describes the control framework - a capital expenditure control system for authorising spend on new assets and projects, with accountability established for implementing projects on time and within the approved budget. Management flags availability of commercially viable real estate at suitable locations, timely execution of sale deeds / leave and license registrations and regulatory approvals, and effective management of store expansion in newer locations, cities and states as the key constraints on the expansion programme. On the funding side, CRISIL reaffirmed a CRISIL AAA/Stable long-term rating on rated bank loan facilities and ICRA assigned [ICRA] A1+ to commercial paper with the limit enhanced from INR 300 crore to INR 500 crore during FY 2025-26.

management_tone.title: Management quality / tone
management_tone.body:
Unusually candid for a first call. Asawa was direct where DMart has historically been vague — he **deliberately put a number (15%) on store growth** ("this time I wanted to be a bit deliberate"), openly said FY26's 85 stores were an *upside surprise* driven by properties readying early rather than a new run-rate, and conceded metro SSSG will not recover. On DMart Ready he was blunt: **"let me be very transparent here… as we've tried to expand into more and more cities, the number of customers acquired were larger, but our losses also grew quite significantly."** That is an admission of a failed expansion, volunteered.

The refusals were consistent and unapologetic rather than evasive — lease economics, DMart Ready AOV and PIN-code growth ("Cannot say. That's a good attempt."), city productivity variance, land-value splits. Notably, an internal correction was made in real time (65 → 68 lease stores) rather than left standing. Vikram Dasu answered the AEL cost question with the specific inflation numbers rather than deflecting.

Where the tone was weakest: the quick-commerce answers were repetitive and market-size-based ("organised trade is in early teens") across at least six questioners, and management admitted it has done no consumer research on switching behaviour and has no view on QC adoption in smaller cities. That is a genuine analytical gap, not just a disclosure choice. The inorganic-QC question was parked at "board level" rather than refused — the one place the door was left open.

risks.title: Risks & watch-items
risks.body:
- **Metro same-store growth is structurally impaired, and management said so.** Cause is a stack: store **maturity/saturation** at high throughput, **deliberate self-cannibalisation** (opening a second store nearby to relieve pressure), and **quick commerce**. On QC's drag: "I'm suspecting that that's **not going to change over the next few years**."
- **Quick-commerce competitive intensity is rising, not plateauing** — Amazon Now and Flipkart Minutes have entered, with analysts citing a 2,000-store Flipkart build-out and ~6,000 dark stores in India. Management's answer was market-size ("early teens" organised share), not a competitive counter-move, and admitted it has done **no work and holds no view** on QC adoption beyond the top 10–12 cities.
- **Pricing-parity erosion.** Analysts report anecdotal price parity with QC platforms online. Management's rebuttal is basket-level saving, but conceded it does not have the like-for-like basket-value trend "right away" and would try to provide it — an evidence gap on the core proposition.
- **Wage code (from Dec-2025) + general wage inflation** is now permanently in the cost base, with no statement that the capability build is complete.
- **Rising leverage with slipping returns** — RoNW 13.5% and ROCE 17.1% both down; borrowing heading to ~INR2,000 cr. If the "self-funding in 2–3 years" claim slips, the equity story changes materially.
- **AEL execution risk** — INR307 cr loss, cost lines inflating 24–34%, and losses that *grew with expansion*. The 11-city model is unproven; a second retreat would be far more damaging than the first.
- **No offline customer data, by choice** — DMart deliberately does not collect store customer data (simplicity/checkout speed), and has run **no consumer study** on customers shifting to QC. It therefore cannot answer whether defectors are visiting less often or buying smaller baskets. That is a real blind spot against data-native competitors.
- **Fresh absence** — competitors (QC platforms, Star Bazaar) position fresh-first; DMart addresses roughly half the retail TAM and has no fresh plan.
- **Real estate is the hard constraint on the entire growth algorithm**, and it is not something capital or headcount can fix.
- **New CEO transition risk** — leadership changes flagged as coming "as superannuation happens or some exits happen," to be announced as they occur.

non_obvious.title: Non-obvious takeaways
non_obvious.body:
- **The 15% benchmark is a downgrade dressed as clarity.** FY26 delivered ~20% store growth (85 adds). Anchoring publicly at 15% resets expectations *down* while sounding like new transparency. And because ~60 of the 85 opened in Q4 FY26, FY27 revenue inherits a full-year kicker from stores that contributed almost nothing to FY26 — so FY27 revenue growth can look fine even as *store adds* decelerate. The optics and the run-rate will diverge.
- **Gross margin is a declared ceiling, not a lever.** Management calls 14–15% "the moat" and commits to passing sourcing gains to customers. Combined with flat revenue per sq ft, that means earnings growth is arithmetically **area × ramp**, with zero contribution from mix, price or private label. Any cost step-up (as with the 33% wage bill) drops straight through to PBT with nothing to offset it. That is a very specific and testable earnings model.
- **DMart has quietly become a leveraged compounder.** "That money is over now" — the 2020 promoter-dilution proceeds are spent, capex now exceeds nothing less than the entire operating cash flow, and borrowing is heading to ~INR2,000 cr. The 2–3-year self-funding promise is the load-bearing assumption in the whole story; if store adds accelerate as promised, self-funding gets *harder*, not easier — the two commitments are in tension.
- **Refusing to collect offline customer data is now a strategic constraint, not just a philosophy.** The new CEO's stated priority is a data and tech overhaul — but he explicitly ring-fenced it away from the customer: data modernisation covers categories, store operations and supply chain, while the store checkout stays anonymous "because one of the values this organization is built around is simplicity." So DMart cannot build personalisation, loyalty or win-back mechanics against QC in stores. Its only customer-identified asset is DMart Ready — the loss-making 11-city business.
- **Self-cannibalisation is now an admitted part of the SSSG number.** Management opens a second store near a saturated one to relieve throughput pressure, "which of course impacts the SSSG." So reported LFL is depressed partly *by DMart's own capex* — a bear on SSSG is partly a bull on area growth, and the two metrics must be read together, never separately.
- **The AEL retreat may be a gift to the quick-commerce incumbents.** Seven cities were vacated because order density was too low — exactly the density problem QC players solve with dark-store scale. DMart has effectively conceded those markets online while its store base keeps expanding into them.
- **The unpulled monetisation lever was named on the record.** "We don't really monetize our app and site experiences, but **that's a big lever at any point in time we can pull**." AEL's path to profitability therefore has an undisclosed ad-revenue option on top of the efficiency plan.
- **The inorganic QC door was left ajar.** Asawa flatly refused instant delivery as an operating model, but on inorganic opportunities or strategic partnerships in quick commerce he deferred to "the board level" — a materially different answer, and the single most interesting non-denial on the call.
- **Avenue Food Plaza is the group's quiet compounder** — +35.5% growth at 9% PAT margin, better than the core retail business's net margin, on adjacencies to existing stores requiring near-zero incremental real estate. It is never discussed as a strategy.

qoq_log.title: QoQ change log (fill each quarter)
qoq_log.body:
- **Q1 FY27 / Annual Analyst Meet 2026 (this):** First call under new MD & CEO **Anshul Asawa** (28-Jul-2026). FY26 closed at **~INR67,000 cr (+16%)**, **EBITDA 7.8% flat**, **PAT INR3,224 cr (4.8%, −25bps)**, **LFL 8.1%**, **500+ stores (85 added, 5 new states)**, **20.6 mn sq ft**, **revenue/sq ft flat at INR33,422**, **~40 cr bill cuts**, **CFO INR4,168 cr vs capex >INR4,000 cr**, **RoNW 13.5% / ROCE 17.1% both down**. Employee cost **+33%** on wage code (Dec-25) + deliberate ahead-of-curve hiring. **New public guidance anchor: ~15% store additions p.a.** (vs ~20% delivered in FY26). **SSSG to hold at ~FY26's 8.1%; metros will not return to double digits.** GM/net-margin North Star reaffirmed at **~15% / ~5%**. **DMart Ready retreated from 18 to 11 cities**, 165 pickup points, sub-6-hour slotted delivery, **AEL net loss INR307 cr** with contract labour +24% and transport +34%; instant delivery ruled out, inorganic QC entry parked "at board level." Balance sheet turns levered: **actual borrowing INR965 cr**, CP ~INR800 cr, **INR1,000 cr NCD approved, may reach ~INR2,000 cr by end-FY27**; claim that existing stores self-fund expansion within **2–3 years**. Lease stores **68 of 500+, 15 added in FY26**. Align Retail PAT +24%; **Avenue Food Plaza +35.5% at 9% PAT margin** (turnaround).
- _Q2 FY27 → check: (1) store adds tracking to ~75 (15%) or slipping; (2) lease share of new adds vs FY26's 15/85; (3) LFL holding at ~8% or breaking below; (4) AEL loss shrinking from INR307 cr and contract-labour/transport lines normalising in the 11-city network; (5) gross margin still inside 14–15% and net margin near 5% despite the wage code; (6) borrowing vs the ~INR2,000 cr ceiling and whether the NCD is issued; (7) whether the employee-cost build is declared complete; (8) any board-level move on inorganic quick commerce; (9) whether the Mumbai fresh pilot scales; (10) whether management ever produces the like-for-like basket-value trend it promised Manoj (ICICI Securities)._

other.title: Notable from the deck
other.body:
- [Subsidiary drag] Avenue E-Commerce Limited (DMart Ready) is still loss-making and deepening: FY26 sales of Rs 4,094 Crs with EBITDA of Rs (185) Crs and PAT of Rs (307) Crs, versus Rs (129) Crs and Rs (247) Crs in FY25.
- [Consolidated gap] Consolidated PAT (Rs 2,970 Crs) is below standalone PAT (Rs 3,224 Crs) in FY26, quantifying the subsidiary drag - chiefly e-commerce - on group earnings.
- [Subsidiaries] Avenue Food Plaza Private Limited (in-store food service) earned Rs 46 Crs PAT on Rs 3,871 Crs sales at a thin 1.86% EBITDA margin, while Align Retail Trades Private Limited (packaged staples) turned around to Rs 9 Crs PAT from a Rs (10) Crs loss, with EBITDA margin expanding to 9.48% from 0.72%.
- [Store disruption] The Sanpada store at Navi Mumbai is closed to customers for reconstruction yet is counted within the 500-store FY26 figure.
- [Context] Employee expense rose 33.5% standalone in FY26 (2.02% of total income vs 1.75%) and finance costs more than doubled, both consistent with the accelerated store build-out.
